Neonates of the Yunnan red-backed vole weigh approximately 2 grams [Wwb = approximately 2 grams] at birth, a modest mass that positions them among the smaller altricial newborns of the Muridae. This initial body size imposes considerable thermoregulatory challenges, as the pups are born hairless and polkilothermic. Field observations suggest that the suckling juveniles are entirely dependent on maternal contact for thermal maintenance during the first week of life. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of a normothermic adult (37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]), the period of nutritional dependence ends relatively early, with weaning occurring at around 12 days after birth [tx = around 12 days after birth]. This rapid transition to independence is a notable feature of the species’ life history, likely reflecting the high extrinsic mortality pressures and seasonal resource pulses characteristic of its montane habitats in Yunnan.

Under the same isothermal conditions of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], females reach sexual maturity at approximately 60 days after birth [tp = approximately 60 days after birth] and gestation lasts approximately 24.5 days [tg = approximately 24.5 days]. This early onset of reproductive capability allows for rapid population turnover, a strategy well-suited to an environment with brief, productive summers. Following successful mating, the duration of pregnancy is similarly compressed, with a relatively short intrauterine development period that aligns with the vole’s altricial mode of reproduction, in which maternal investment is shifted toward postnatal lactation rather than prolonged in utero growth. The combination of early puberty and swift gestation enables females to produce multiple cohorts within a single breeding season.

Upon reaching adulthood, the maximum body mass of this species stabilizes at about 60 grams [Wwi = about 60 grams], a figure that represents the upper end of the size range documented across its geographic distribution. This adult mass, modest even by murid standards, has direct implications for the animal’s energetics. Basal metabolic rate, measured via respirometry at the species’ typical core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], reaches a maximum of 79.57 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 79.57 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This level of oxygen consumption is consistent with the allometric expectations for a small rodent of this body size, though it may be slightly elevated compared to strictly fossorial or arid-adapted relatives, potentially reflecting the metabolic demands of its cool, high-elevation environment. Captive studies indicate that the maximum lifespan is about 2008 days [am = about 2008 days], or roughly 5.5 years, when individuals are maintained at that temperature, though survival in the wild is almost certainly much at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] lower.

Reproductive output is structured around a modest litter size: females typically produce 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = 7 pups per litter]. Under optimal conditions, with a prolonged breeding season, females may produce up to three litters annually [F_R_i = up to three litters annually]. This combination of moderate fecundity per event and multiple reproductive iterations within a year yields a considerable annual reproductive output, allowing populations to rebound quickly following periods of low density. The interplay between litter size and breeding frequency appears finely tuned to the vole’s short lifespan; few individuals persist beyond several breeding episodes.

The species’ life history is thus characterized by a syndrome of rapid development and early, repeated reproduction. The earliest reproductive events, facilitated by the attainment of puberty at 60 days after birth [tp = 60 days after birth], are critical for population persistence in unpredictable montane environments at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The efficient allocation of resources is underscored by a brief nursing period—weaning at 12 days after birth [tx = 12 days after birth]—which frees the mother to invest in subsequent litters with minimal inter-birth interval at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. A short gestation of 24.5 days [tg = 24.5 days] further compresses the reproductive cycle at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Although individual lifespan may theoretically extend to approximately 2008 days [am = approximately 2008 days] in the laboratory at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], field mortality is high, and the combination of early puberty, rapid weaning, and multiple annual litters appears adaptive for a rodent that must balance high reproductive demands against a finite adult mass of around 60 grams [Wwi = around 60 grams].
